# STAT 847 extension: EasyEnsemble {#sec-ensemble}

## Idea and implementation

Under-sampling was the only remedy that clearly improved the forest's ROC-AUC
in the simulation, but it throws away most of the data: at 1% prevalence it
keeps about 2% of the training rows. EasyEnsemble [@liu2009] keeps the
benefit and recovers the waste. It draws $B$ different under-sampled training
sets, each with all the positives and a *different* random set of negatives,
fits a model to each, and averages their predicted probabilities. Each member
trains on balanced data, and together the members see most of the negatives.
This is the "combine weak learners into a stronger one" idea from the
ensemble-learning part of the course (learning objective 6 for STAT 847):
each under-sampled model is noisy, and averaging reduces that noise, as
bagging does for trees [@islr2, Section 8.2.1].

Our implementation (`R/ensemble.R`) uses $B = 10$ members and the same two
classifiers as the rest of the study, so the comparison is fair. The original
paper uses boosting inside each member; we did not, so that any difference
comes from the ensembling and not from a new learner. For the forest, each
member has 20 trees, so the ensemble has the same 200 trees in total as a
single forest. The members are trained on 50:50 data, so we classify at 0.5.
The ensemble is run on exactly the same simulated data sets and real-data
splits as the other methods (its seeds continue after the twelve methods'
seeds), so we can compare it replicate by replicate.

**What to compare with.** A new method should beat the best existing one, not
the baseline. In every setting we compared the ensemble with the *best*
single approach for that classifier and measure, chosen as the one with the
highest mean in that setting. Choosing the best after seeing the results
favours the single approach, so this comparison is conservative for the
ensemble. As before, we count a difference only if it exceeds 2 MCSE and
0.005.

## Results

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ens-count
#| tbl-cap: "EasyEnsemble against the best single approach in each of the 12 imbalanced simulation settings (prevalence 20%, 5% or 1%), counted only if the difference exceeds 2 MCSE and 0.005."
es <- read.csv("results/table_ensemble_sim.csv")
es <- es[es$prev < 0.5, ]
es$verdict <- ifelse(grepl("negligible|no clear", es$verdict), "no real difference", es$verdict)
es$metric <- c(roc.auc = "ROC-AUC", pr.auc = "PR-AUC", bal.accuracy = "Balanced accuracy")[es$metric]
es$classifier <- ifelse(es$classifier == "logistic", "Lasso logistic", "Random forest")
ct <- as.data.frame.matrix(table(paste(es$classifier, "|", es$metric),
                                 factor(es$verdict, levels = c("ensemble better",
                                        "no real difference", "best single better"))))
ct <- cbind(Classifier = sub(" \\|.*", "", rownames(ct)),
            Measure = sub(".*\\| ", "", rownames(ct)), ct)
names(ct)[3:5] <- c("Ensemble better", "No real difference", "Best single better")
kable(ct, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE, align = "llccc")
```

@fig-ens shows the size of the differences and @tbl-ens-count counts them.

![EasyEnsemble minus the best single approach in each setting, paired on the same data sets and pooled over separation (200 replicates per point), bars $\pm 2$ MCSE. Above zero means the ensemble is better.](figures/fig7_ensemble_vs_best.png){#fig-ens width=85%}

**Forests: a consistent gain in ROC-AUC and balanced accuracy.** For the
random forest the ensemble beats the best single approach on ROC-AUC in 11 of
the 12 imbalanced settings, and on balanced accuracy in 11 of 12. The gain
grows as positives become rarer, up to about 0.03 at 1% prevalence and
$n = 1{,}000$. This fits our explanation of why under-sampling helps a forest
(@sec-sim-rank): each member breaks the ties of the baseline forest, and
averaging ten members trained on different negatives removes much of the
noise that a single under-sampled forest suffers from.

**PR-AUC: mixed.** For PR-AUC the ensemble is better in some forest settings
and worse in others, and at 1% prevalence and $n = 20{,}000$ it loses about
0.015 to the best single approach. Like under-sampling, it gives high
probabilities to many negatives, which hurts precision at the top of the
ranking.

**Lasso: no gain.** For the lasso the ensemble is never better than the best
single approach and is worse at 1% prevalence and $n = 1{,}000$, where each
member is fitted to only about 20 rows. This is what we should expect. The
lasso is a stable, low-variance method, and here a correct one, so there is
little variance for averaging to remove, while each member pays the full cost
of under-sampling.

**Real data.** @tbl-ens-real compares the ensemble with the best single
approach on the credit card data.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ens-real
#| tbl-cap: "Real data: EasyEnsemble against the best single approach for each classifier and measure, mean over 10 splits (SE of the paired difference)."
er <- read.csv("results/table_ensemble_real.csv")
er$metric <- c(roc.auc = "ROC-AUC", pr.auc = "PR-AUC", bal.accuracy = "Balanced accuracy")[er$metric]
er$classifier <- ifelse(er$classifier == "logistic", "Lasso logistic", "Random forest")
er$best.approach <- c(oversample = "Over-sampling", smote = "SMOTE", threshold = "Threshold",
                      undersample = "Under-sampling", baseline = "Baseline",
                      weights = "Class weights")[er$best.approach]
names(er) <- c("Measure", "Classifier", "Best single approach", "EasyEnsemble",
               "Best single", "Difference")
kable(er, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE, align = "lllrrr")
```

On the real data the ensemble ties with the best single approach on ROC-AUC
and balanced accuracy, and loses about 0.08 PR-AUC to the best single
approach for both classifiers. So the ensemble does not rescue the lasso's
PR-AUC on real data, and it does not beat forest + SMOTE.

## What we learned

EasyEnsemble helps the learner that needs it: an unstable, flexible model
facing very few positives. There, averaging several under-sampled models
improves the ranking beyond any single remedy. It does not help a stable and
correctly specified model, and it inherits under-sampling's weakness on
PR-AUC and calibration. In line with the rest of the report, it changes the
forest's ranking for the better but, for the lasso, it is one more way to move
the operating point.
